title: Complex Resistor Networks: Series-Parallel Combinations
tagline: Stepwise network simplification, nodal analysis, and equivalent resistance calculations.
theoryHtml:
1. Mixed Series-Parallel Resistor Circuits

Real-world electronic circuits rarely consist of pure series or pure parallel configurations; instead, they feature intricate mixed combinations. To determine the overall equivalent resistance ($R_\text{eq}$) of such a network, we apply a methodical reduction strategy:

  1. Identify Inner Pure Groups: Look for pairs or sub-groups of resistors that are connected strictly in series (carrying identical current) or strictly in parallel (connected across identical nodes).
  2. Replace with Equivalent Resistors: Calculate the sub-equivalent resistance ($R_s = R_1 + R_2$ or $R_p = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$) and redraw the circuit replacing the group with a single equivalent resistor.
  3. Iterate Stepwise: Repeat the simplification from the inside out until the entire circuit collapses into a single master equivalent resistor.

2. Classic Bridge and Delta Configurations

Consider two parallel branches containing series pairs: Branch 1 has $R_1 + R_2$ and Branch 2 has $R_3 + R_4$. First compute the series sum of each branch, then solve the two resulting branches in parallel:

$$R_\text{eq} = \frac{(R_1 + R_2)(R_3 + R_4)}{(R_1 + R_2) + (R_3 + R_4)}$$
pointsToRemember: Simplify complex networks by isolating and reducing inner pure series and parallel sub-blocks.
Two series resistors in parallel: $R_\text{eq} = \frac{R_A \cdot R_B}{R_A + R_B}$ where $R_A = R_1 + R_2$ and $R_B = R_3 + R_4$.
Always trace current paths from node to node to confirm series vs parallel relationships.
keyNotes: Resistors are in series ONLY if they carry identical current without any branch tapping off between them; resistors are in parallel ONLY if both their terminals share identical common pairs of nodes.

questions.question: An electric heater of resistance 44 Ω draws 5 A from service mains for 2 hours. What is the rate at which heat is developed in the heater?
questions.explanation: The 'rate of heat development' means power: P = I²R = (5 A)² × 44 Ω = 25 × 44 = 1100 W = 1100 J/s.

questions.question: A uniform cylindrical wire of resistance R is STRETCHED uniformly until its length becomes THREE TIMES (3l) its original length. What is its new resistance?
options: 9R (volume is constant, so area becomes A/3)
questions.answer: 9R (volume is constant, so area becomes A/3)
questions.explanation: Volume V = l × A is constant. If length triples (l' = 3l), area becomes A' = A/3. R' = ρ(3l)/(A/3) = 9 ρ(l/A) = 9R.

questions.question: A piece of wire of resistance R is cut into FIVE equal parts. These five parts are then connected in parallel. If the equivalent resistance of this parallel combination is R', what is the ratio R / R'?
questions.explanation: Each piece has resistance r = R/5. When 5 pieces of R/5 are in parallel: R' = (R/5)/5 = R/25. Thus R / R' = 25.

questions.question: Two conducting wires of identical material, length, and diameter are connected across the same voltage source, first in series and then in parallel. What is the ratio of heat produced in series to parallel combination in a given time (H_series : H_parallel)?
questions.explanation: For constant V: H = (V²/R)t. Rs = 2R, Rp = R/2. H_series / H_parallel = (V²/(2R)) / (V²/(R/2)) = (1/2) / 2 = 1/4 (1 : 4).

questions.question: How can three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω be connected to give an equivalent total resistance of 4 Ω?
options: Connect 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel, and place this combination in series with the 2 Ω resistor
Connect 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series, in parallel with 6 Ω
questions.answer: Connect 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel, and place this combination in series with the 2 Ω resistor
questions.explanation: 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel give Rp = (3 × 6)/(3 + 6) = 18/9 = 2 Ω. In series with the 2 Ω resistor: Req = 2 Ω + 2 Ω = 4 Ω.

questions.question: How can three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω be connected to give an equivalent total resistance of 1 Ω?
options: Connect all three resistors in parallel
Connect all three resistors in series
Connect 2 Ω and 6 Ω in series, in parallel with 3 Ω
Connect 2 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel, in series with 6 Ω
questions.answer: Connect all three resistors in parallel

questions.question: Four resistors each of resistance 4 Ω are connected to form the four sides of a square ABCD. What is the equivalent resistance between two diagonally opposite corners A and C?
questions.explanation: Path ABC has 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. Path ADC has 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. These two 8 Ω branches are in parallel between A and C: Req = 8/2 = 4 Ω.

questions.question: In the square resistor circuit above (four 4 Ω sides), what is the equivalent resistance between two adjacent corners A and B?
questions.explanation: Branch 1 is side AB (4 Ω). Branch 2 is path AD + DC + CB = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 Ω. In parallel: Req = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 48/16 = 3 Ω.

questions.question: What is the minimum resistance that can be obtained using four resistors each of 1/4 Ω?
questions.explanation: Minimum resistance is achieved by connecting all in parallel: Rp = R / n = (1/4) / 4 = 1/16 Ω.

questions.question: What is the maximum resistance that can be obtained using four resistors each of 1/4 Ω?
questions.explanation: Maximum resistance is obtained by connecting all in series: Rs = 4 × (1/4 Ω) = 1 Ω.

title: The Heating Effect of Electric Current: Molecular Mechanism
tagline: Electron-lattice inelastic collisions, dissipation of electrical work, and thermal energy conversion.
theoryHtml:
1. Why Does an Electric Conductor Get Warm?

When an electric cell or battery is connected across a conductor, its chemical reactions maintain a potential difference ($V$) that establishes an electric field. This field exerts electrostatic forces on the conduction electrons, accelerating them along the conductor.

2. Microscopic Collision Mechanism

As the free electrons drift towards the positive terminal:

  • They continually collide inelastically with the fixed, vibrating metallic lattice ions and atoms.
  • At each collision, the electrons transfer a portion of their kinetic energy to the lattice ions.
  • This transferred energy amplifies the amplitude of thermal vibrations of the lattice ions.
  • Macroscopically, increased lattice vibration manifests as a rise in the temperature of the conductor—the heating effect of electric current (also termed Joule heating).

3. Energy Conversion Perspective

If an electric circuit is purely resistive (consisting purely of resistors and battery with no mechanical motors):

$$\text{Chemical Energy of Battery} \longrightarrow \text{Electrical Energy} \longrightarrow \mathbf{100\%\text{ Thermal Heat Dissipation}}$$

All the electrical work performed by the battery is steadily dissipated into the surroundings as heat.
pointsToRemember: Drifting electrons collide with metallic lattice ions, transferring kinetic energy into thermal vibrations.
Heating effect of electric current (Joule heating) converts electrical work into thermal energy.
In a purely resistive circuit, all electrical energy supplied by the source is converted entirely into heat.
keyNotes: While Joule heating is deliberately utilized in toasters and geysers, it represents an undesirable energy loss (called $I^2R$ copper loss) in electric motors, computers, and power grid transmission lines.

questions.question: A copper wire has a diameter of 0.5 mm and resistivity of 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What length of this wire is required to obtain a resistance of 10 Ω?
In the above copper wire of resistance 10 Ω, if the diameter of the wire is DOUBLED while keeping length unchanged, what will be the new resistance?
questions.explanation: Area A ∝ d². Doubling diameter quadruples area (A' = 4A). Since R ∝ 1/A, R' = R / 4 = 10 Ω / 4 = 2.5 Ω.

questions.question: An electric iron consumes 840 W at maximum heating and 360 W at minimum heating from a 220 V source. What are the resistance values of the iron in each case?
At the microscopic level, what directly generates heat when electric current flows through a metallic wire?
options: Friction between air molecules and the outside of the insulation
Inelastic collisions between drifting conduction electrons and the vibrating positive ions of the metal lattice
Chemical reaction between electrons and protons
questions.answer: Inelastic collisions between drifting conduction electrons and the vibrating positive ions of the metal lattice
questions.explanation: Electrons accelerated by the electric field collide with lattice ions, transferring kinetic energy into thermal vibrations.

questions.question: In a purely resistive electrical circuit containing only a resistor and a battery, into what form of energy is all electrical energy converted?
questions.explanation: Without mechanical motors or storage capacitors, 100% of electrical energy is dissipated as heat into the surroundings.

questions.question: In which of the following electrical devices is the heating effect of current an UNDESIRABLE wasteful energy loss?
questions.explanation: In motors and microprocessors, Joule heating wastes energy and requires cooling fans to prevent thermal failure.

questions.question: What is the term given to the energy lost as heat in long-distance electrical power transmission cables?
questions.explanation: The continuous dissipation of electrical energy as heat in conducting wires due to internal resistance is known as I^2R loss.

questions.question: How do electrical grid utilities minimize I^2R heating losses when transmitting power over hundreds of kilometres?
options: By transmitting electricity at extremely high voltages (e.g., 400 kV) to minimize the current I
By cooling power lines with liquid nitrogen
By turning off electricity at night
questions.answer: By transmitting electricity at extremely high voltages (e.g., 400 kV) to minimize the current I
questions.explanation: Since P = VI, transmitting at very high voltage lowers current I drastically; since heat H ∝ I^2, energy losses are minimized.

questions.question: If a current I flows through a resistor of resistance R for time t under potential difference V, what is the work done W by the source?
questions.explanation: W = V × Q. Since Q = I × t, W = V × I × t = I^2Rt.

questions.question: Why does a laptop or mobile phone become noticeably warm when running heavy applications or charging?
options: The battery emits infrared laser beams
High current flowing through the internal resistance of the microprocessor and battery dissipates heat via Joule's effect
The screen reflects body heat back into the phone
questions.answer: High current flowing through the internal resistance of the microprocessor and battery dissipates heat via Joule's effect
questions.explanation: Rapid switching of billions of transistors and high charging currents generate thermal dissipation (P = I^2R).

title: Joule's Law of Heating: Mathematical Derivation ($H = I^2Rt$)
tagline: Proportionality to I^2, R, and t; alternate formulas VIt and V^2t/R.
theoryHtml:
1. Derivation of Joule's Law

Consider a current $I$ flowing through a resistor of resistance $R$ across which a potential difference $V$ is maintained for a time $t$:

  • The total electric charge transported in time $t$ is $Q = I \cdot t$.
  • The work done ($W$) in moving charge $Q$ across potential difference $V$ is: $$W = V \cdot Q = V \cdot (I \cdot t) = V I t$$
  • By Ohm's law, $V = I \cdot R$. Substituting $V$ into the work equation gives: $$W = (I \cdot R) \cdot I \cdot t = \mathbf{I^2 R t}$$

Assuming all electrical energy is dissipated as thermal energy, the heat generated ($H$) is:

$$\mathbf{H = I^2 R t}$$

2. The Three Formal Laws of Joule's Heating

  1. Current Law: Heat generated is directly proportional to the square of the current ($H \propto I^2$) for a given resistance. (Doubling current quadruples heat!).
  2. Resistance Law: Heat generated is directly proportional to the resistance of the conductor ($H \propto R$) for a given current.
  3. Time Law: Heat generated is directly proportional to the time for which current flows ($H \propto t$).

3. Alternate Equivalent Mathematical Expressions

$$H = I^2 R t = V I t = \frac{V^2}{R} t$$

Note on application: Use $H = I^2Rt$ for series circuits (constant current); use $H = \frac{V^2}{R}t$ for parallel circuits (constant voltage).
pointsToRemember: Joule's Law of Heating: $H = I^2Rt = VIt = \frac{V^2}{R}t$.
Heat is proportional to the square of current ($I^2$): doubling $I$ produces $4\times$ more heat.
In series (constant $I$), higher $R$ generates more heat; in parallel (constant $V$), lower $R$ generates more heat!
keyNotes: Beware of the classic exam trap: for domestic parallel appliances on 220V, heat is inversely proportional to resistance ($H \propto 1/R$), so low-resistance appliances produce the most heat!

questions.question: Which of the following mathematical expressions correctly represents electric power (P)?
questions.explanation: By Ohm's law substitutions: P = VI = I(IR) = I²R = V(V/R) = V² / R.

questions.question: Compare the power consumed in the 2 Ω resistor in two circuits: Circuit 1 (6 V battery in series with 1 Ω and 2 Ω resistors) and Circuit 2 (4 V battery in parallel with 12 Ω and 2 Ω resistors):
options: Circuit 1: 4 W; Circuit 2: 4 W (Both consume equal power = 8 W)
Circuit 1: P₁ = 8 W; Circuit 2: P₂ = 8 W (Equal power of 8 W in both)
questions.answer: Circuit 1: P₁ = 8 W; Circuit 2: P₂ = 8 W (Equal power of 8 W in both)
questions.explanation: Circuit 1: I = 6 V / (1 + 2) = 2 A. P₁ = I²R = (2 A)² × 2 Ω = 8 W. Circuit 2: V across 2 Ω is 4 V. P₂ = V²/R = 4²/2 = 16/2 = 8 W. Both consume exactly 8 W.

questions.question: A battery of 9 V is connected in series with resistors of 0.2 Ω, 0.3 Ω, 0.4 Ω, 0.5 Ω, and 12 Ω. What is the current flowing through the 12 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation: Total series resistance Rs = 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 + 0.5 + 12 = 13.4 Ω. In series, current is identical everywhere: I = V / Rs = 9 / 13.4 = 0.6716 A ≈ 0.67 A.

questions.question: According to Joule's Law of Heating, what happens to the heat produced in a resistor if the current flowing through it is DOUBLED while resistance and time remain constant?
questions.explanation: Since H ∝ I^2, doubling current (2I)^2 = 4I^2, which quadruples the heat generated.

questions.question: Which of the following mathematical expressions correctly represents Joule's Law of Heating?
questions.explanation: Joule's law states that thermal energy generated is H = I^2 R t.

questions.question: 100 Joules of heat is produced each second in a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the resistor?
An electric iron of resistance 20 Ω takes a current of 5 A. What is the heat developed in 30 seconds?
Between two resistors of 5 Ω and 10 Ω connected in SERIES across a battery, which resistor produces MORE heat?
options: The 10 Ω resistor produces more heat because current is constant (H = I^2 R t => H ∝ R)
The 5 Ω resistor produces more heat
questions.answer: The 10 Ω resistor produces more heat because current is constant (H = I^2 R t => H ∝ R)
questions.explanation: In series, identical current flows through both, so heat is directly proportional to resistance (H ∝ R).

questions.question: Between two resistors of 5 Ω and 10 Ω connected in PARALLEL across a 220 V supply, which resistor produces MORE heat?
options: The 5 Ω resistor produces more heat because voltage is constant (H = (V^2 / R) t => H ∝ 1/R)
The 10 Ω resistor produces more heat
Heat production depends on atmospheric pressure
questions.answer: The 5 Ω resistor produces more heat because voltage is constant (H = (V^2 / R) t => H ∝ 1/R)
questions.explanation: In parallel, both receive identical voltage (220 V), so heat is inversely proportional to resistance (H ∝ 1/R).

questions.question: What is the SI unit of heat energy dissipated by an electric circuit?
questions.explanation: Heat is a form of energy; its standard SI unit is the joule (J).

title: Practical Thermal Applications: Electric Iron, Heater & Nichrome
tagline: Heating elements, alloy advantages: high resistivity, high melting point, and oxidation resistance.
theoryHtml:
1. Practical Domestic Heating Appliances

The heating effect of electric current is harnessed in indispensable household appliances such as electric irons, room heaters, water geysers, toasters, and electric kettles. All these appliances incorporate an internal metallic coil known as the heating element.

2. Why Nichrome Alloy is the Material of Choice

Pure copper or silver is never used for heating elements. Instead, an alloy—most notably Nichrome (composed of $60\%\text{ Nickel}$, $16\%\text{ Chromium}$, $23\%\text{ Iron}$, and $1\%\text{ Manganese}$)—is exclusively employed for three crucial engineering reasons:

  1. High Electrical Resistivity ($\rho \approx 100 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot\text{m}$): Roughly 60 times higher than that of copper. This allows compact heating coils to achieve high resistance ($R$) without requiring absurdly long wires.
  2. Extremely High Melting Point (~$1400^\circ\text{C}$): Can operate red-hot without melting.
  3. Resistance to Oxidation (Does Not Burn): Unlike pure metals that rapidly oxidize and vaporize when red-hot in atmospheric air, nichrome forms a tough, self-passivating chromium oxide outer film that prevents further oxidation even at $900\text{--}1000^\circ\text{C}$.

3. Why Does the Heating Element Glow While the Cord Does Not?

The connecting power cord is made of thick, low-resistance copper wire, whereas the heating element is a coiled, thin, high-resistance nichrome wire:

  • Because they are in series, the exact same current ($I$) flows through both the power cord and the heating element.
  • By Joule's law ($H \propto R$), heat generated in the low-resistance copper cord ($R_\text{copper} \approx 0.01\ \Omega$) is negligible, so it stays cool.
  • In contrast, the high resistance of the nichrome element ($R_\text{element} \approx 50\ \Omega$) generates immense heat, causing it to become red-hot and glow brilliantly!
pointsToRemember: Heating appliances (electric iron, toaster, geyser) utilize high-resistance heating elements.
Nichrome alloy (Ni-Cr-Fe-Mn) has high resistivity, high melting point, and does not oxidize at red-hot temperatures.
The heating element glows red-hot because its resistance is huge ($H \propto R$), while the low-resistance copper cord stays cool.
keyNotes: Mica sheets are placed inside electric irons to insulate the red-hot nichrome heating element from the metallic soleplate because mica is an excellent conductor of heat but an exceptional insulator of electricity!

questions.question: What is the commercial unit of electrical energy consumed in households (commonly called a 'unit' on electric bills)?
questions.explanation: The commercial billing unit of electrical energy is kilowatt-hour (kWh).

questions.question: How many Joules (J) are equal to ONE KILOWATT-HOUR (1 kWh)?
How many 10 W, 220 V electric lamps can be safely connected in parallel across a 220 V line if the maximum permissible fuse current is 5 A?
questions.explanation: Total allowable power P_total = V × I_max = 220 V × 5 A = 1100 W. Number of 10 W lamps = 1100 W / 10 W = 110 lamps.

questions.question: Why does the heating element of an electric room heater glow red-hot while the connecting power cord does not?
options: The cord has a separate battery
The connecting cord is made of thick low-resistance copper that produces negligible heat (H ∝ R), whereas the heating element has very high resistance and becomes red-hot
The cord is kept in liquid nitrogen
The current only flows inside the heating element
questions.answer: The connecting cord is made of thick low-resistance copper that produces negligible heat (H ∝ R), whereas the heating element has very high resistance and becomes red-hot
questions.explanation: Because current is identical in series, Joule heating H ∝ R ensures that the high-resistance nichrome element gets scorching hot while the copper cord stays cool.

questions.question: What is the chemical composition of the alloy Nichrome used in heating elements?
questions.explanation: Nichrome is an alloy consisting of approximately 60% Nickel, 16% Chromium, 23% Iron, and 1% Manganese.

questions.question: Why are alloys like Nichrome preferred over pure metals for electrical heating devices?
options: Alloys have higher resistivity and do not oxidize (burn) readily even at high red-hot temperatures
questions.answer: Alloys have higher resistivity and do not oxidize (burn) readily even at high red-hot temperatures
questions.explanation: Nichrome combines high resistivity with remarkable oxidation resistance at incandescent temperatures (~1000°C).

questions.question: Why is a sheet of natural Mica used to sandwich the heating element in a domestic electric iron?
options: Mica is a good thermal conductor of heat, but a superb electrical insulator, conducting heat to the baseplate while preventing electric shocks
Mica produces pleasant perfume when heated
questions.answer: Mica is a good thermal conductor of heat, but a superb electrical insulator, conducting heat to the baseplate while preventing electric shocks
questions.explanation: Mica conducts heat efficiently to the soleplate while insulating the user from lethal electrical current.

questions.question: What is the approximate melting point of Nichrome alloy?
questions.explanation: Nichrome melts at approximately 1400°C, enabling it to glow red-hot (~900°C) safely without melting.

questions.question: If an electric toaster draws 4 A of current on a 220 V line, what is the resistance of its internal heating element?
What happens if a heating element made of pure copper wire is connected to a 220 V mains supply?
options: It glows with green light forever
Due to extremely low resistance, it draws massive current, burns out, melts, and causes a dangerous short circuit
questions.answer: Due to extremely low resistance, it draws massive current, burns out, melts, and causes a dangerous short circuit
questions.explanation: Low resistance copper across 220V causes an extreme current spike that instantly melts the wire and trips the breaker.

title: The Incandescent Electric Bulb: Tungsten Filament & Inert Gases
tagline: Thermal incandescence, extreme melting point (3380°C), and inactive Argon/Nitrogen atmosphere.
theoryHtml:
1. Principle of Incandescence

An incandescent electric bulb generates light by heating a thin metallic filament to such an extreme temperature that it becomes white-hot and emits electromagnetic thermal radiation in the visible spectrum (incandescence). However, only about $5\text{--}10\%$ of electrical energy is converted into visible light; the remaining $90\text{--}95\%$ is dissipated as invisible infrared heat radiation!

2. Why Tungsten ($W$) is Exclusively Used for Bulb Filaments

Tungsten is the only metal suited for incandescent filaments due to unmatched physical properties:

  • Extremely High Melting Point ($3380^\circ\text{C}$): The highest melting point of any metallic element on the periodic table. It can glow at dazzling white-hot temperatures (~$2500\text{--}2700^\circ\text{C}$) without melting.
  • High Resistivity & Ductility: Can be drawn into ultra-thin, long coiled-coil filaments to maximize resistance and surface area in a tiny glass bulb.

3. Why are Bulbs Filled with Chemically Inactive Gases?

If air were present inside the glass bulb, atmospheric oxygen would react instantly with the white-hot tungsten filament, burning it to tungsten oxide and destroying the bulb in a split second. To prevent this:

  • The glass bulb is evacuated and filled with chemically non-reactive, inert gases—principally Argon mixed with some Nitrogen.
  • The inert gas pressure suppresses the thermal vaporization (sublimation) of tungsten atoms from the filament, significantly prolonging the operational lifespan of the bulb.
pointsToRemember: Tungsten has an extraordinarily high melting point of $3380^\circ\text{C}$ and high tensile ductility.
Incandescent bulbs convert only $\sim 5\text{--}10\%$ of electrical energy into light; the rest is lost as heat.
Bulbs are filled with inactive Argon and Nitrogen to prevent oxidation and retard filament evaporation.
keyNotes: Because of their poor energy efficiency (~90% wasted as heat), incandescent tungsten bulbs have been largely superseded by compact fluorescent lamps (CFLs) and modern solid-state light-emitting diodes (LEDs).

questions.question: A current of 0.5 A flows through the filament of an electric bulb for 10 minutes. What is the total electric charge that flows through the circuit?
How much work (W) is done in moving a charge of 2 C across two points having a potential difference of 12 V?
When a 12 V battery is connected across an unknown resistor, a current of 2.5 mA flows through it. What is the resistance of the resistor?
Which metal is exclusively used for making the filament of traditional incandescent electric lamps?
questions.explanation: Tungsten is used because of its extraordinary melting point of 3380°C, allowing it to glow white-hot without melting.

questions.question: What is the melting point of Tungsten metal?
questions.explanation: Tungsten has the highest melting point among all metals at 3380°C.

questions.question: Which chemically inactive gases are typically filled inside an incandescent bulb to prolong filament life?
questions.explanation: Argon and nitrogen are chemically unreactive gases that prevent tungsten oxidation and suppress filament evaporation.

questions.question: What happens immediately if an incandescent light bulb develops a hairline crack that lets atmospheric air enter the bulb?
options: The bulb glows twice as bright
The white-hot tungsten filament oxidizes (burns) instantly in oxygen and snaps, destroying the bulb
questions.answer: The white-hot tungsten filament oxidizes (burns) instantly in oxygen and snaps, destroying the bulb
questions.explanation: Hot tungsten reacts violently with atmospheric oxygen to form volatile tungsten oxide, burning out the filament in milliseconds.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of electrical energy consumed by a traditional incandescent bulb is actually converted into useful visible light?
questions.explanation: Traditional incandescent bulbs are notoriously inefficient; roughly 90-95% of energy is wasted as invisible infrared heat.

questions.question: Why is the tungsten filament wound into a tight 'coiled-coil' helical shape inside the bulb?
options: To make it fit into a small glass bulb while maintaining a long length (high resistance) and reducing cooling by gas convection
To act as a spring against earthquakes
Because straight wires cannot conduct current
questions.answer: To make it fit into a small glass bulb while maintaining a long length (high resistance) and reducing cooling by gas convection
questions.explanation: Coiling packs a long thin filament into a compact space, raising resistance and trapping heat to maintain incandescence.

questions.question: Why have modern Solid-State LED (Light Emitting Diode) bulbs largely replaced traditional incandescent tungsten bulbs?
options: LEDs produce cold laser light that cures skin diseases
LEDs convert over 80% of electrical energy into light with minimal heat loss, consuming far less power and lasting 25 times longer
Incandescent bulbs emit radiation that attracts insects only
questions.answer: LEDs convert over 80% of electrical energy into light with minimal heat loss, consuming far less power and lasting 25 times longer
questions.explanation: LEDs emit light via quantum bandgap recombination rather than heat incandescence, providing massive energy savings.

title: The Electric Fuse: Working Principle, Current Rating & Circuit Safety
tagline: Sacrificial circuit protection, low melting point alloy, series placement on live wire.
theoryHtml:
1. What is an Electric Fuse?

An electric fuse is an indispensable safety device inserted into an electrical circuit to protect delicate appliances and domestic building wiring against catastrophic damage caused by overloading or short-circuiting.

2. Physical Construction & Material Properties

A fuse consists of a piece of thin wire made of a metallic alloy having:

  • Low Melting Point: Typically made of an alloy of lead ($63\%$) and tin ($37\%$), or tin-plated copper.
  • Appropriate Resistance: Sufficient to heat up rapidly if current exceeds safety thresholds.
  • Enclosed inside a fireproof cartridge of porcelain, ceramic, or glass with metal end-caps.

3. How Does a Fuse Operate?

The fuse is always connected in SERIES with the LIVE wire ahead of any appliance:

  1. Under normal conditions, circuit current is below the fuse's rated capacity; heat dissipated is safely conducted away.
  2. If a fault occurs—such as a short circuit (direct contact between live and neutral wires) or overloading (too many high-power appliances switched on simultaneously)—current spikes dangerously.
  3. By Joule's law ($H \propto I^2$), the excessive current instantly raises the fuse wire temperature past its melting point.
  4. The fuse wire melts, burns apart, and breaks the circuit in milliseconds, cutting off power before wires can catch fire or appliances explode!

4. Standard Current Ratings

Fuses are rated in amperes according to the maximum safe current they can carry without blowing: $1\text{ A}, 2\text{ A}, 3\text{ A}, 5\text{ A}, 10\text{ A}, 15\text{ A}, 16\text{ A}$.
pointsToRemember: An electric fuse protects circuits by melting when current exceeds its designated rating.
Fuse wire has a LOW melting point (alloy of lead and tin).
A fuse is ALWAYS connected in SERIES with the LIVE wire ahead of appliances.
keyNotes: Never replace a blown fuse with a thick copper wire or iron nail! A copper wire will not melt during a fault, causing house wiring to overheat and trigger catastrophic electrical fires.

questions.question: How much energy is given to each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery?
questions.explanation: Energy W = V × Q = 6 V × 1 C = 6 J.

questions.question: An electric bulb of resistance 1200 Ω is connected to a 220 V supply. How much current does it draw?
What happens to the electrical resistance and resistivity of a metallic conductor when its temperature INCREASES?
options: Both resistance and resistivity increase due to increased thermal vibrations of metal lattice ions colliding with drifting electrons
questions.answer: Both resistance and resistivity increase due to increased thermal vibrations of metal lattice ions colliding with drifting electrons
questions.explanation: Increasing temperature intensifies ionic lattice vibrations, increasing electron collision frequency and raising both resistance and resistivity.

questions.question: What is the primary function of an electric fuse in a household electrical circuit?
options: To increase the voltage of the battery
To break the circuit automatically by melting when current exceeds safe limits, preventing fire and appliance damage
To regulate the colour of lights
questions.answer: To break the circuit automatically by melting when current exceeds safe limits, preventing fire and appliance damage
questions.explanation: A fuse is a sacrificial protective device that melts under excessive current to isolate the circuit.

questions.question: What key physical property must the wire used in an electric fuse possess?
options: Low melting point and suitable resistance
questions.answer: Low melting point and suitable resistance
questions.explanation: A low melting point ensures the fuse wire melts quickly before building wires can overheat.

questions.question: In which domestic wire must an electric fuse always be connected?
options: In series with the Live (Phase) wire
In parallel with the Neutral wire
In series with the Earth wire
questions.answer: In series with the Live (Phase) wire
questions.explanation: Connecting in series with the live wire ensures that when the fuse blows, high mains voltage is completely isolated from the appliance.

questions.question: An electric iron consumes 1 kW (1000 W) of electric power when operated at 220 V. What rating fuse must be installed in its circuit?
questions.explanation: Current I = P / V = 1000 W / 220 V = 4.54 A. The next standard fuse rating above 4.54 A is 5 A.

questions.question: What common alloy is used to manufacture safety fuse wire?
questions.explanation: A lead-tin alloy is used because of its low eutectic melting point (~183°C) and stable conductivity.

questions.question: Why is it extremely dangerous to replace a blown fuse with a thick copper wire or an iron nail?
options: Copper wire absorbs too much moisture
Thick copper wire has a high melting point and will not melt during a fault, allowing excessive current to cause electrical fires
Copper wire causes the bulb to turn green
questions.answer: Thick copper wire has a high melting point and will not melt during a fault, allowing excessive current to cause electrical fires
questions.explanation: Bypassing the fuse with heavy copper disables protection; massive fault currents will overheat wires and ignite walls.

questions.question: What is the difference between an 'overload' and a 'short circuit'?
options: A short circuit occurs when live and neutral wires touch directly with near-zero resistance; overloading occurs when total current drawn by multiple appliances exceeds safe wiring limits
Short circuit happens only in summer
questions.answer: A short circuit occurs when live and neutral wires touch directly with near-zero resistance; overloading occurs when total current drawn by multiple appliances exceeds safe wiring limits
questions.explanation: Short circuit is direct wire-to-wire contact (zero resistance); overloading is cumulative excessive load from too many running appliances.

title: Electric Power: Definitions, Formulas ($P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$) & The Watt
tagline: Rate of electrical energy consumption, SI unit Watt (W), and kilowatt conversions.
theoryHtml:
1. Definition of Electric Power ($P$)

Electric power is defined as the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or dissipated into other forms of energy (such as heat, light, or mechanical motion) in an electric circuit:

$$P = \frac{\text{Electrical Energy Consumed }(W)}{\text{Time Interval }(t)} = \frac{V \cdot I \cdot t}{t}$$ $$\mathbf{P = V \cdot I}$$

2. The Three Equivalent Formulas for Electric Power

By substituting Ohm's law ($V = IR$ or $I = V/R$), we obtain three master equations:

  1. $$P = V \cdot I$$ (Useful when both voltage and current are known)
  2. $$P = I^2 \cdot R$$ (Useful for series circuits where current $I$ is constant)
  3. $$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ (Useful for parallel circuits where voltage $V$ is constant)

3. The SI Unit: The Watt ($\text{W}$)

The SI unit of electric power is the watt (W), named in honour of Scottish engineer James Watt:

"1 watt is the power consumed by a device that draws 1 ampere of current when operated at a potential difference of 1 volt ($1\text{ W} = 1\text{ Volt} \times 1\text{ Ampere} = 1\text{ V}\cdot\text{A}$)."

Larger multiple units:

  • $1\text{ kilowatt (kW)} = 1000\text{ W} = 10^3\text{ W}$
  • $1\text{ megawatt (MW)} = 10^6\text{ W}$
  • $1\text{ gigawatt (GW)} = 10^9\text{ W}$
pointsToRemember: Electric power is the rate of electrical energy consumption: $P = W/t$.
Master power equations: $P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$.
The SI unit of power is the Watt ($1\text{ W} = 1\text{ V}\cdot\text{A} = 1\text{ J/s}$); $1\text{ kW} = 1000\text{ W}$.
keyNotes: For appliances operating on the fixed 220V domestic supply, power is inversely proportional to resistance ($P = V^2/R$); a high-power 2000W geyser has much lower resistance than a 60W bulb!

questions.question: An electric heater coil of resistance 100 Ω is connected to a 220 V supply. How much current does it draw?
An electric heater draws 4 A when connected to a 60 V line. What current will it draw if the potential difference is increased to 120 V?
questions.explanation: R = V₁ / I₁ = 60 V / 4 A = 15 Ω. At 120 V: I₂ = V₂ / R = 120 V / 15 Ω = 8 A.

questions.question: A uniform wire of resistance R is bent into the shape of a closed CIRCLE. What is the effective resistance between two diametrically opposite points A and B on the circle?
questions.explanation: The circle splits into two semicircular halves of resistance R/2 connected in parallel: R_eff = (R/2) / 2 = R/4.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT represent electrical power in a circuit?
questions.explanation: P = VI = I^2 R = V^2 / R. The expression I R^2 has units of Volts-Ohms and does not represent power.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of electrical power?
questions.explanation: The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.

questions.question: An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. When it is operated on 110 V, what is the power consumed?
Between two bulbs rated '220 V, 100 W' and '220 V, 40 W', which bulb's filament has the GREATER electrical resistance?
options: The 40 W bulb has greater resistance because R = V^2 / P (resistance is inversely proportional to power)
questions.answer: The 40 W bulb has greater resistance because R = V^2 / P (resistance is inversely proportional to power)
questions.explanation: Since R = V^2/P, lower rated power means higher filament resistance: R_40 = 1210 Ω vs R_100 = 484 Ω.

questions.question: What is the resistance of an electric lamp that draws a current of 0.5 A from a 220 V line, and what is its power?
Define 1 Watt of electric power in terms of volts and amperes:
options: The power consumed by a device that carries 1 Ampere when operated at 1 Volt
The power dissipated by a 1 Ohm resistor in 1 hour
questions.answer: The power consumed by a device that carries 1 Ampere when operated at 1 Volt
questions.explanation: 1 Watt = 1 Volt × 1 Ampere (1 W = 1 V·A = 1 J/s).

questions.question: 1 kilowatt (1 kW) is equivalent to how many watts?
questions.explanation: The prefix 'kilo' represents 1000, so 1 kW = 1,000 W.

title: Commercial Unit of Electrical Energy: The Kilowatt-Hour (kWh)
tagline: The Board of Trade Unit, 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J, and domestic meter recording.
theoryHtml:
1. Why is the Joule Impractical for Electricity Billing?

The SI unit of energy, the joule (J), represents the energy consumed by a tiny $1\text{-watt}$ appliance in just $1\text{ second}$ ($1\text{ J} = 1\text{ W}\cdot\text{s}$). Because modern households operate powerful appliances (air conditioners, geysers, refrigerators) consuming millions of joules daily, measuring electricity in joules would result in astronomically large, unwieldy numbers on electricity bills.

2. The Commercial Unit: The Kilowatt-Hour ($\text{kWh}$)

To provide a convenient, practical commercial scale, electricity utilities measure electrical energy in kilowatt-hours (kWh), commonly referred to simply as "units" of electricity (or Board of Trade Unit, B.O.T.U.):

"1 kilowatt-hour is the amount of electrical energy consumed by an appliance of 1000 watts (1 kW) power rating running continuously for 1 hour."

3. Converting Kilowatt-Hours to Joules

$$\begin{aligned} 1\text{ kWh} &= 1\text{ kilowatt} \times 1\text{ hour} \\ &= 1000\text{ watts} \times 3600\text{ seconds} \\ &= 3,600,000\text{ watt-seconds} \\ &= \mathbf{3.6 \times 10^6\text{ Joules}} \end{aligned}$$ $$\mathbf{1\text{ unit} = 1\text{ kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6\text{ J} = 3.6\text{ MJ}}$$
pointsToRemember: The commercial unit of electrical energy is the kilowatt-hour ($\text{kWh}$), commonly termed a 'unit'.
$1\text{ kWh}$ is the energy consumed by a $1\text{ kW}$ appliance operating for 1 hour.
Conversion factor: $\mathbf{1\text{ kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6\text{ J}}$.
keyNotes: Electricity meters installed outside homes record energy consumption in kilowatt-hours (units), which forms the basis of monthly utility billing.

questions.question: An electric lamp of resistance 20 Ω and a series resistor of 4 Ω are connected to a 6 V battery. What is the total circuit resistance and current?
questions.explanation: Rs = 20 Ω + 4 Ω = 24 Ω. Current I = V / Rs = 6 V / 24 Ω = 0.25 A.

questions.question: Three resistors of 5 Ω, 10 Ω, and 30 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the equivalent resistance of the combination?
Two electric bulbs rated 220 V, 40 W and 220 V, 100 W are connected in SERIES across a 220 V supply. Which bulb will glow BRIGHTER?
options: The 40 W bulb (it has higher filament resistance and dissipates more I²R power in series)
questions.answer: The 40 W bulb (it has higher filament resistance and dissipates more I²R power in series)
questions.explanation: R = V²/P ⇒ R₄₀ > R₁₀₀. In series, I is identical, so heat P = I²R is greater in the 40 W bulb, making it glow brighter.

questions.question: What is the commercial unit of electrical energy recorded on household electric meters?
questions.explanation: Electricity utilities measure and bill domestic energy in kilowatt-hours (kWh), commonly termed 'units'.

questions.question: How many Joules are equivalent to 1 kilowatt-hour (1 kWh)?
How long must a 100 W light bulb burn continuously to consume exactly 1 unit (1 kWh) of electrical energy?
questions.explanation: Energy = Power × time => 1 kWh = 0.1 kW × t => t = 1 / 0.1 = 10 hours.

questions.question: An electric refrigerator rated 400 W operates 8 hours/day. What is the electrical energy consumed by the refrigerator in 30 days?
questions.explanation: Daily energy = 400 W × 8 h = 3200 Wh = 3.2 kWh. For 30 days: 3.2 kWh × 30 = 96 kWh (96 units).

questions.question: Why is the kilowatt-hour (kWh) a unit of ENERGY rather than a unit of power?
options: Because kilowatt is power, and multiplying by time (hours) yields energy (Energy = Power × Time)
It is a unit of power, not energy
questions.answer: Because kilowatt is power, and multiplying by time (hours) yields energy (Energy = Power × Time)
questions.explanation: Power = Energy / Time, therefore Energy = Power × Time. Kilowatt (power) × Hour (time) = Energy.

questions.question: Convert 250 units (250 kWh) of electrical energy into Joules:
If a household consumes 10 kWh of electricity in a day, how many Joules of energy were used?

title: Electricity Billing: Power Ratings, Consumption & Cost Estimation
tagline: Systematic calculation of total units consumed, tariff rates, and monthly utility bills.
theoryHtml:
1. Systematic Electricity Bill Calculation Protocol

To calculate the electricity bill for a household over a billing period (e.g., 30 days):

  1. List All Appliances: For each appliance type, note its power rating in watts ($P$), the quantity of appliances ($N$), and daily operating hours ($t$).
  2. Calculate Daily Energy Consumption: $$E_\text{daily (Wh)} = N \times P\text{ (Watts)} \times t\text{ (hours/day)}$$
  3. Convert to Kilowatt-Hours (Units): $$\text{Units per day (kWh)} = \frac{E_\text{daily (Wh)}}{1000}$$
  4. Calculate Total Monthly Units: $$\text{Total Units} = \text{Daily Units} \times \text{Number of days in month (e.g., 30)}$$
  5. Calculate Financial Cost: $$\text{Total Cost (Rs.)} = \text{Total Units (kWh)} \times \text{Tariff Rate (Rs. per unit)}$$

2. Worked Example

A household operates the following appliances daily:

  • 4 LED tubes of $20\text{ W}$ each for $5\text{ hours}$: $4 \times 20 \times 5 = 400\text{ Wh}$
  • 2 ceiling fans of $80\text{ W}$ each for $10\text{ hours}$: $2 \times 80 \times 10 = 1600\text{ Wh}$
  • 1 refrigerator of $250\text{ W}$ running $24\text{ hours}$ (compressor active 10 hrs): $250 \times 10 = 2500\text{ Wh}$
  • Total daily consumption $= 400 + 1600 + 2500 = 4500\text{ Wh} = 4.5\text{ kWh (units)}$.
  • Consumption in 30 days $= 4.5 \times 30 = \mathbf{135\text{ units}}$.
  • At a rate of $\text{Rs. } 6.00\text{ per unit}$, monthly cost $= 135 \times 6.00 = \mathbf{\text{Rs. } 810.00}$.
pointsToRemember: Energy in $\text{kWh} = \frac{\text{Power in Watts} \times \text{Time in hours}}{1000}$.
Total energy = sum of energies of all running appliances.
Cost = Total $\text{kWh (units)} \times \text{Cost per unit (tariff)}$.
Convert minutes to hours and watts to kilowatts before calculating bills.
keyNotes: Energy conservation directly lowers utility bills: replacing a 100W incandescent bulb with a 10W LED saves 90% of electricity for identical illumination!

questions.question: Two electric bulbs rated 220 V, 40 W and 220 V, 100 W are connected in PARALLEL across a 220 V supply. Which bulb will glow BRIGHTER?
options: The 100 W bulb (it draws more current and consumes full rated power P = V²/R = 100 W)
questions.answer: The 100 W bulb (it draws more current and consumes full rated power P = V²/R = 100 W)
questions.explanation: In parallel, both receive 220 V, so the 100 W bulb consumes its full 100 W rating and glows brighter than the 40 W bulb.

questions.question: If a 0.1% increase in length is produced in a wire by stretching, what is the approximate percentage change in its electrical resistance?
questions.explanation: For small fractional stretching with constant volume: R ∝ l² ⇒ ΔR/R ≈ 2(Δl/l) = 2(0.1%) = +0.2%.

questions.question: In an electric circuit, five identical resistors of resistance R are connected in a symmetrical bridge network. If the bridge is balanced, what is the equivalent resistance across the main terminals?
options: R (no current flows through the central bridging resistor)
questions.answer: R (no current flows through the central bridging resistor)
questions.explanation: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge (R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄ = 1), potential across the bridge is zero (no current through central R). Equivalent is two parallel branches of 2R: Rp = (2R)/2 = R.

questions.question: A 2 kW electric geyser is used for 2 hours every day. At a tariff of Rs. 5.00 per unit, what is the cost of operating the geyser for 30 days?
questions.explanation: Daily energy = 2 kW × 2 h = 4 kWh. 30 days energy = 4 × 30 = 120 kWh (units). Total cost = 120 units × Rs. 5 = Rs. 600.

questions.question: Five 60 W bulbs are used for 4 hours daily, and three 100 W fans are used for 10 hours daily. What is the total energy consumed in a 30-day month?
questions.explanation: Bulbs: 5 × 60 W × 4 h = 1200 Wh. Fans: 3 × 100 W × 10 h = 3000 Wh. Daily total = 4200 Wh = 4.2 kWh. Monthly = 4.2 × 30 = 126 kWh.

questions.question: What is the cost of running the appliances in the problem above for 30 days at Rs. 4.00 per unit?
questions.explanation: Total units = 126 kWh. Cost = 126 × Rs. 4.00 = Rs. 504.00.

questions.question: How many units of electricity are saved in 30 days by replacing a 100 W incandescent bulb with a 10 W LED bulb, operating 10 hours each day?
questions.explanation: Power saved = 100 W - 10 W = 90 W = 0.09 kW. Daily energy saved = 0.09 kW × 10 h = 0.9 kWh. 30 days: 0.9 × 30 = 27 kWh.

questions.question: An electric heater rated 1500 W operates for 3 hours. How many units of electricity did it consume?
questions.explanation: Energy = 1.5 kW × 3 h = 4.5 kWh = 4.5 units.

questions.question: If an electric toaster consumes 2.2 kWh of energy in a week, how many Joules of energy did it consume?
A student runs a 50 W laptop for 6 hours a day for an entire 30-day month. At Rs. 6.00 per unit, what is the cost on the electric bill?
questions.explanation: Daily energy = 50 W × 6 h = 300 Wh = 0.3 kWh. Monthly = 0.3 × 30 = 9 kWh. Cost = 9 × Rs. 6.00 = Rs. 54.00.

title: Comprehensive Electricity Review: Circuits, Resistors & Power Mastery
tagline: Synthesis of Ohm's law, series/parallel combinations, Joule heating, and power formulas.
theoryHtml:
1. Master Summary of Governing Formulas in Electricity

Physical QuantityFormula(s)SI Unit
Electric Current ($I$)$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{n e}{t} = \frac{V}{R}$Ampere (A)
Potential Difference ($V$)$V = \frac{W}{Q} = I \cdot R$Volt (V)
Resistance ($R$)$R = \rho \frac{l}{A} = \rho \frac{l}{\pi r^2}$Ohm ($\Omega$)
Resistivity ($\rho$)$\rho = R \frac{A}{l}$Ohm-metre ($\Omega\cdot\text{m}$)
Series Resistance$R_s = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$Ohm ($\Omega$)
Parallel Resistance$\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}$Ohm ($\Omega$)
Joule's Heating ($H$)$H = I^2 R t = V I t = \frac{V^2}{R} t$Joule (J)
Electric Power ($P$)$P = V I = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R} = \frac{W}{t}$Watt (W)
Commercial Energy$E = P\text{ (kW)} \times t\text{ (h)}$$\text{kWh}$ ($= 3.6 \times 10^6\text{ J}$)

2. Expert Problem-Solving Guidelines

  • In series circuits, current $I$ is constant; voltage splits ($V = V_1 + V_2$).
  • In parallel circuits, voltage $V$ is constant; current splits ($I = I_1 + I_2$).
  • Always ensure units are converted into SI standard base units ($\text{A, V, }\Omega\text{, s, m}$) before calculation!
pointsToRemember: Mastery of $V = IR$, $R = \rho l/A$, and series/parallel equations solves $90\%$ of board numericals.
Joule heating: $H = I^2Rt$; Power: $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$.
Commercial energy is measured in $\text{kWh}$ ($1\text{ unit} = 3.6 \times 10^6\text{ J}$).
keyNotes: Always check whether appliances are in series or parallel before picking the power formula: use $P = I^2R$ for series and $P = V^2/R$ for parallel!

questions.question: Why does the statement 'Electrons are consumed in an electric circuit' represent a fundamental physical misconception?
options: Electrons are charge carriers that circulate continuously without being destroyed; what is consumed is the potential energy provided by the electric source
Electrons are only present in batteries
questions.answer: Electrons are charge carriers that circulate continuously without being destroyed; what is consumed is the potential energy provided by the electric source
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved; electrons merely transport electrochemical energy from source to load where it is converted to thermal/kinetic work.

questions.question: An ammeter has a resistance of 0.02 Ω. If it is erroneously connected in PARALLEL across a 12 V battery, what will occur?
options: It measures the battery voltage accurately
An enormous short-circuit current (I = 12/0.02 = 600 A) flows through the low-resistance ammeter, burning out the meter coil immediately
questions.answer: An enormous short-circuit current (I = 12/0.02 = 600 A) flows through the low-resistance ammeter, burning out the meter coil immediately
questions.explanation: Due to negligible internal resistance, connecting an ammeter in parallel short-circuits the battery, causing destructive overcurrent.

questions.question: A voltmeter has an extremely high internal resistance of 100,000 Ω. If it is accidentally connected in SERIES in a torch circuit, what happens?
options: The huge series resistance drops the circuit current almost to zero, so the bulb fails to glow while the voltmeter reads the full battery voltage
questions.answer: The huge series resistance drops the circuit current almost to zero, so the bulb fails to glow while the voltmeter reads the full battery voltage
questions.explanation: The high resistance of the voltmeter in series throttles circuit current, stopping bulb illumination while recording battery EMF.

questions.question: Three identical resistors connected in series consume 10 W of power from a DC source. If the same three resistors are reconnected in PARALLEL across the same source, what power will they consume?
questions.explanation: Rs = 3R ⇒ P_s = V² / (3R) = 10 W ⇒ V²/R = 30 W. In parallel: Rp = R/3 ⇒ P_p = V² / (R/3) = 3(V²/R) = 3 × 30 W = 90 W.

questions.question: If the current flowing through a fixed ohmic resistor increases by 100% (doubles), what is the percentage increase in the power dissipated in the resistor?
options: 300% increase (power quadruples to 4P, an increase of 300%)
questions.answer: 300% increase (power quadruples to 4P, an increase of 300%)
questions.explanation: P ∝ I². Doubling current (I' = 2I) makes P' = (2I)²R = 4 I²R = 4P. Percentage increase = ((4P - P)/P) × 100% = 300%.

questions.question: A wire of resistance R is cut into 'n' equal parts, and all 'n' parts are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of this combination?
questions.explanation: Each part has resistance r = R/n. Parallel of n such parts gives R_eq = r / n = (R/n) / n = R / n².

questions.question: Why does the resistivity of semiconductors (like silicon and germanium) DECREASE with rising temperature, unlike metallic conductors?
options: Thermal energy breaks covalent bonds, exponentially increasing the concentration of free electron-hole charge carriers
questions.answer: Thermal energy breaks covalent bonds, exponentially increasing the concentration of free electron-hole charge carriers
questions.explanation: In semiconductors, thermal carrier generation dominates over lattice scattering, dramatically decreasing resistivity (negative temperature coefficient).

questions.question: An electric kettle has two heating coils. When coil 1 is used alone, water boils in 10 minutes. When coil 2 is used alone, water boils in 15 minutes. If both coils are connected in PARALLEL, how long will it take to boil the same water?
questions.explanation: Heat required H is constant. Power P = H/t = V²/R ⇒ 1/t ∝ 1/R. In parallel, 1/Rp = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ ⇒ 1/t = 1/t₁ + 1/t₂ ⇒ t = (10 × 15)/(10 + 15) = 150/25 = 6 mins.

questions.question: In the same electric kettle, if both coils (10 min and 15 min) are connected in SERIES, how long will it take to boil the water?
questions.explanation: In series: Rs = R₁ + R₂. Since t ∝ R (from H = (V²/Rs)t): t = t₁ + t₂ = 10 min + 15 min = 25 min.

questions.question: Two electric bulbs rated 60 W, 220 V and 100 W, 220 V are connected in PARALLEL to a 220 V mains supply. What is the total current drawn from the line?
questions.explanation: Total power P = 60 + 100 = 160 W. Since in parallel, V = 220 V. Total current I = P / V = 160 W / 220 V ≈ 0.727 A ≈ 0.73 A.
